title: Hades: The Unseen King
summary: A lunar month with Hades, ruler of the dead, approached with the care the Greeks themselves took: the god whose name they avoided, his rare cult as Plouton, the rules of chthonic offering, and nine quiet nights of remembrance that end in a dedication.
welcome:
This is a month of study and careful devotion with Hades, the Greek god who rules the dead. He is not the devil, not death itself and not the villain of films. He is the stern, just king of the world below, brother of Zeus, husband of Persephone, and, as Plouton, the giver of the wealth that comes up out of the earth.

The Greeks rarely worshipped him. They spoke of him with euphemisms, offered to him with averted faces, and never shared what they gave him. This journey keeps that care. It is quieter and more sparing than most, and that is the point.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation, and it does not make you a priest of anything. If you are grieving, Hades can be a steady presence; if you find yourself drawn to him because you are thinking about ending your life, please stop and talk to someone now: a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line such as 988 in the US or Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, or your local emergency number. You will need a small lamp, a bowl of water, a dish of earth or a place outside to pour, and honey, milk and water.
about: In Greek myth, after the gods defeated the Titans, the three sons of Kronos drew lots for the world: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades “the darkness of the realms under the earth,” as Poseidon puts it in the Iliad. His name may mean “the unseen,” and he wore a cap of invisibility. He rules the dead with Persephone, whom he carried off from her mother, and he is grim and unyielding: the Iliad calls him the god most hateful to mortals because he never gives anyone back. Yet he is not evil. He keeps the laws of the dead, punishes oath-breakers, and is fair. Few Greeks built him temples; Pausanias says the Eleans were the only people he knew of who honoured Hades with one, and it opened once a year. Instead people called him Plouton, “the wealthy one,” who sends up grain and metal from below, or Zeus Katachthonios, Zeus of the underworld, and honoured him beside Persephone at Eleusis and in cave shrines. Offerings to him were poured into the earth at night and never eaten. The Romans knew him as Pluto and Dis Pater. Today a small number of Hellenic polytheists honour him, mostly as Plouton and alongside Persephone, and he has many modern devotees drawn by grief, death work and pop culture. This journey asks you to meet the ancient god, not the cartoon.
notes: Offerings to Hades are chthonic. They are poured into the earth, a pit or a dish of soil, or burnt or left, and are never eaten, drunk or shared. Keep his dishes separate from kitchen ware.
Ancient Greeks often avoided his name and called him Plouton or another title. You may do the same; many modern devotees do.
Hades is not Thanatos (Death), not Satan, and not a villain. Modern films, games and comics have reshaped him; this journey separates those from the ancient god.
If thoughts of your own death are part of what draws you here, please speak to a doctor, a counsellor or a crisis line first. Devotion to the king of the dead is not a way toward him.
Keep any offering of honey, wine or food left outside away from places pets and wildlife can reach, and never leave grapes, raisins, onion or chocolate out.

stages.title: At the edge of the ground
stages.intro: Hades was approached at the earth itself, at night, with lowered hands. So the journey begins outside or at a dish of soil, after dark, with a short, respectful introduction. You are introducing yourself, not asking for anything.

practices.title: Find a place to pour
practices.instructions: Before the opening rite, find the place where you will pour Hades’s libations this month. The best is bare earth: a garden bed, the foot of a tree, a corner of a park you can reach after dark safely. If you have none, choose a large plant pot or set aside a deep dish filled with soil, used for nothing else. Spend a few minutes there in daylight, quietly.
practices.prompt: How did it feel to choose a place for the god below? What did I notice about the ground?

rite.title: An introduction at the earth
rite.summary: A short, sober introduction after dark: purify, begin with Hestia, lower your hands toward the earth, greet Hades by a respectful title, and pour honey-milk and water into the ground without sharing.

ingredients.name: A bowl of fresh water for khernips
A match, or a sprig of bay or rosemary to quench in it
A small lamp, tealight or electric candle
A small cup of milk with a spoonful of honey stirred in
Bare earth outside, a plant pot, or a dish of soil kept for him
A sprig of cypress, or of fresh mint

rite.preparation: Do this after dark. Wash your face and hands in ordinary water first. Dress plainly. If you are going outside, tell someone where you are and take a torch. Set the lamp, the two cups and the khernips where you will kneel or crouch.

steps.title: Make khernips
steps.instructions: Light the match or the tip of the bay sprig and plunge it into the bowl of water. Wash your hands in it and touch a few drops to your face.
steps.spoken: With clean hands I come to the edge of the ground.

steps.title: Begin with Hestia
steps.instructions: Light the lamp. Speak to Hestia first, as every Greek rite does. She belongs to the house above; you are about to turn to the world below.
steps.spoken: Hestia, first and last, keeper of the hearth, I begin with you.

steps.title: Lower your hands
steps.instructions: Kneel or crouch. Lay your palms flat on the earth or on the soil, or turn them downward just above it. Greeks prayed to the gods below this way, and some struck the ground to be heard. Keep your voice low. Use the title Plouton if you prefer not to say his name.
steps.spoken: Plouton, Hades, unseen king, lord of the many below, brother of Zeus and husband of Persephone: I am [your name]. I come with respect, to learn who you are. I ask nothing tonight.

steps.title: Pour into the earth
steps.instructions: Pour the honey-milk slowly into the ground, then the water. Turn your face a little aside as you pour, as Greeks did for the powers below. Do not drink any of it, and do not keep any back.

steps.title: Sit in quiet
steps.instructions: Sit for a few minutes in silence. Let nothing come if nothing comes.

steps.title: Turn back to the house
steps.instructions: Stand up. Wash your hands again in the khernips. Turn back toward the house and speak Hestia’s name. Put out the lamp.
steps.spoken: Hestia, last as you were first. I return to the living.

rite.closing: Leave the libation in the ground. If you used a dish of soil indoors, take it outside the next day and tip it onto earth, then clean the dish and keep it for his use only. Pour the khernips away outside. Before going to bed, do something ordinary and living: eat, drink a glass of water, speak to someone. Write a few lines about what it was like to kneel at the ground.
rite.safety: Never leave a flame unattended, and use a lantern or an electric candle outside. If you go out after dark, tell someone and stay in safe, lit places. Wash your hands after handling soil.

stages.title: The house of Hades
stages.intro: About ten days of reading, one lesson every two or three days. First who Hades is, and who he is not; then his myths; then how the Greeks approached him and why so rarely. Read slowly. This is a god people took seriously.

lessons.title: The unseen king
lessons.summary: His place among the gods, his names and euphemisms, his emblems, and what he is not.

sections.heading: The third share
sections.body:
Hades is the eldest son of Kronos and Rhea, swallowed at birth with his siblings and rescued by Zeus. In the Iliad, Poseidon explains how the brothers divided the world: “We were three brothers whom Rhea bore to Saturn—Jove, myself, and Hades who rules the world below.” (The translator Samuel Butler used the Roman names for Kronos and Zeus.) They cast lots: Poseidon got the sea, Zeus the sky, and “Hades took the darkness of the realms under the earth.” The earth and Olympus were shared.

So Hades is not a lesser god. He is one of the three great powers of the universe, with his own kingdom and his own laws. In Homer his realm is called “the house of Hades,” and in time the place itself took his name.

sections.heading: Names they did not say
sections.body:
Greeks were wary of saying his name. They used titles instead, and these titles tell you how they saw him. Plouton, “the wealthy one,” became the most common, because all the riches of the earth come from below: seed corn, metals, the dead themselves, who are many. Klymenos means “renowned,” Eubouleus “good counsellor,” and Polydegmon or Polydektes “receiver of many.” The Homeric Hymn to Demeter calls him “the Son of Cronos, He who has many names,” “Host of Many” and “Ruler of Many.”

Homer also calls him Zeus Katachthonios, Zeus of the underworld, and Hesiod tells farmers to pray to “Zeus of the Earth,” whom most readers take to be the same god below. Aidoneus is a poetic form of his name. The Romans called him Pluto, from Plouton, and Dis Pater, “rich father.” When you pray, it is perfectly traditional to use Plouton or another title.

sections.heading: Emblems
sections.body:
He was rarely shown in Greek art, and when he was, he looked much like Zeus: a mature, bearded king, enthroned, holding a sceptre. As Plouton he holds a cornucopia, a horn overflowing with fruit and grain. He sometimes holds a key, because he keeps the gates of the underworld locked; the Orphic Hymn to Pluto says “Earth’s keys to thee, illustrious king belong.” His cap of invisibility, the kynee, was lent to others in myth; Athena wears it in the Iliad.

Cerberus, the many-headed dog, guards his gate so that the dead cannot leave. Black animals, especially rams and bulls, were sacrificed to him. His plants include the cypress, planted in cemeteries; the white poplar; mint, from the story of Minthe; asphodel, the pale flower of the meadows of the dead; and the narcissus and pomegranate from his wife’s story.

sections.heading: What he is not
sections.body:
Hades is not death itself. Death is Thanatos, the winged son of Night, who fetches the dying. Hades rules those already dead. He is not the judge of souls either; that was Minos, Rhadamanthys and Aiakos in later sources. And he is not a devil. Greek religion had no god of evil. Hades does not tempt or torment people for pleasure. Punishments in the underworld, like those of Sisyphus and Tantalos, are for great crimes against the gods.

He is also not the sarcastic villain of the 1997 Disney Hercules, nor the brooding romantic of modern comics, nor the troubled father of the video game Hades, though many people first meet him there. Those are new characters with an old name. The ancient Hades is quieter and stranger: stern, just, unmoving, and not unkind.

knowAndDont.known: The division by lot is in Iliad 15. His titles Plouton, Klymenos, Eubouleus, Polydegmon and Zeus Katachthonios are attested in Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymn and inscriptions. His emblems in art (sceptre, cornucopia, key) and his rare depiction are well documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: The meaning of the name Hades is debated: “the unseen” is an old explanation, but not certain. Plouton may have begun as a separate god of wealth who merged with Hades. How much ordinary Greeks feared him, rather than simply respecting his domain, is hard to judge.

lessons.inPractice: Many Hellenic polytheists address him only as Plouton, and keep any image of him small and apart from the main household shrine. Decide now which name you will use this month. If you are unsure, use Plouton; it is the respectful old choice.
reflect: Where did your picture of Hades come from? Films, games, books, myths?
How do you feel about a god whose name people avoided out of respect?
further: Homer, Iliad 15.185–195, trans. Samuel Butler (1898), Project Gutenberg #2199
Walter Burkert, Greek Religion (1985), section on Hades and the chthonic gods
Daniel Ogden (ed.), A Companion to Greek Religion (2007)

lessons.title: The king who does not give back
lessons.summary: The marriage to Persephone, the rule of no return, and the heroes who went down.

sections.heading: Persephone
sections.body:
The best-known myth of Hades is the taking of Persephone, told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter. With Zeus’s consent, and without asking the girl or her mother, Hades rides out of the earth and carries her off. When Zeus orders her return, Hades gives her a pomegranate seed so that she must come back to him for part of each year. It is not a gentle story, and modern retellings that turn it into a romance are modern.

But the hymn also shows Hades speaking to Persephone with respect. He tells her he will be “no unfitting husband” and that she will rule all that lives and moves below and have the greatest honours. In later myth and art they rule together as a royal pair, faithful to each other in a way Zeus never is. Most ancient worship of Hades was with Persephone, not alone.

sections.heading: Ruthless and unyielding
sections.body:
The defining quality of Hades in Homer is that he does not give back. In the Iliad, Agamemnon says “it is only Hades who is utterly ruthless and unyielding—and hence he is of all gods the one most hateful to mankind.” He is hated not for cruelty but for finality. Nobody returns. Prayers and gifts do not move him.

This is why stories of people who went down and tried to bring someone back are so powerful. Orpheus charmed Hades and Persephone with his music and was allowed to lead his wife Eurydice back, on condition he did not look behind him; he looked, and lost her. Herakles went down and dragged Cerberus up into the light, then took him back. Theseus and Peirithoos went down to steal Persephone and were trapped on chairs of forgetfulness. Odysseus, more wisely, did not go in at all: he dug a pit at the edge and called the dead to him.

sections.heading: The giver of wealth
sections.body:
Hades has another side. As Plouton he is the god of the riches below the earth. Grain is stored and sown in the ground. Metals and gems are dug from it. In Athenian art Plouton holds a cornucopia, and he was honoured beside Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis, perhaps as the god who receives the seed in autumn and sends up the harvest.

Plato, in the dialogue Cratylus, has Socrates argue that people fear the name Hades for no good reason, and that Plouton is a better name because he gives wealth, and the wisest kind of wealth: the dead are freed from the body’s desires. That is philosophy, not cult, but it shows that some Greeks thought about Hades with something closer to gratitude than fear.

sections.heading: What the myths ask
sections.body:
Together, these stories teach a few plain things. Death is final. The dead should be honoured, not called back. There are laws in the world below, and the gods who keep them are fair. And there is wealth in what goes into the ground: grief can become something that feeds the living.

For a devotee, this means approaching Hades without either fear or flirtation. He is not a monster to be appeased or a lover to be won. He is a king to be respected, a keeper of your dead, and the god of the one thing nobody escapes. Many people find, to their surprise, that this is deeply steadying.

knowAndDont.known: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter gives the abduction and Hades’s promise of honours. Iliad 9 calls him ruthless and unyielding. Orpheus, Herakles, Theseus and Odysseus’s descents are told in Virgil, Ovid, Apollodorus and the Odyssey. Plato’s Cratylus (403a–404b) discusses his names.
knowAndDont.unknown: The Orpheus and Eurydice story with the backward glance is known mainly from Roman poets, Virgil and Ovid; earlier Greek versions may have ended differently. Whether Plouton’s role at Eleusis meant he was part of the Mysteries is not known.

lessons.inPractice: Some devotees keep the lesson of Orpheus as a rule: in devotion to Hades, honour your dead but do not try to call them back or hold them. Write down the names of the dead you would like him to keep well this month, on a card you will keep on his shrine.
reflect: What does it mean to you that Hades never gives back?
Is there wealth that has come out of something you buried or lost?
further: Homer, Iliad book 9 and Odyssey book 11, trans. Samuel Butler, Project Gutenberg
Virgil, Georgics 4, on Orpheus and Eurydice

lessons.title: The rare cult: how Hades was approached
lessons.summary: Why he had so few temples, the shrine at Elis, the Plutonia, the pit and the averted face.

sections.heading: Almost no temples
sections.body:
Greek cities were full of temples to Zeus, Athena, Apollo and Demeter. Temples to Hades were almost unknown. The travel writer Pausanias, in the second century CE, says the people of Elis were the only ones he knew of who honoured Hades with a sanctuary. It was opened once a year, and even then only the priest was allowed to enter; Pausanias guesses this is because people too go down to Hades only once. The Eleans explained that when Herakles attacked Pylos, Hades had fought against him, and they honoured the god as a friend and an enemy of Herakles.

There was also a sanctuary at the foot of Mount Minthe in Triphylia, named after the nymph in the mint story, and a few others. But for the most part Hades was not given the ordinary cult of sacrifices and feasts. He was the god you did not need to court. Sooner or later, everyone came to him.

sections.heading: Plutonia and Plouton
sections.body:
Where Hades was honoured, it was usually as Plouton and with Persephone. At Eleusis, beside the hall of the Mysteries, a small cave shrine called the Plutonion was sacred to them. Other Plutonia, caves and chasms believed to be entrances to the underworld, were known across the Greek world. At Hierapolis in Asia Minor a cave gave off poisonous gas that killed birds and animals; the priests of Kybele were said to enter unharmed. Archaeologists rediscovered it in 2013.

Inscriptions show that Plouton was sometimes offered a couch and a table in Athens, a ritual meal laid for a god, and that he was honoured with the Two Goddesses. So the Greeks did not ignore him. They approached him through his wife, through his gentler name, and at the places where the earth seemed to open.

sections.heading: The pit and the pour
sections.body:
The clearest description of how to approach the powers below comes from the Odyssey. Circe tells Odysseus to “dig a trench a cubit or so in length, breadth, and depth, and pour into it as a drink-offering to all the dead, first, honey mixed with milk, then wine, and in the third place water—sprinkling white barley meal over the whole.” Then black sheep are sacrificed with their heads turned toward Erebus, and burnt with prayers “to Hades and to Proserpine,” while Odysseus himself turns away.

This is the pattern of chthonic offering. It happens at night. It goes down into the earth, into a pit the Greeks called a bothros, rather than up in smoke from a raised altar. Animals were black and burnt whole, not shared as a feast. Worshippers lowered their hands, beat the ground, or turned their faces aside. Nothing given was taken back.

sections.heading: Rome: Dis and the mundus
sections.body:
The Romans honoured Dis Pater and Pluto in a similar way. Offerings were made at night, black animals were sacrificed, and libations were poured onto the ground. In the older, Republican form of the Secular Games, held roughly once a century, sacrifices were made to Dis and Proserpina at an underground altar in the Campus Martius called the Tarentum, uncovered only for the festival. Augustus’s Games of 17 BCE used the same place but honoured the Fates and other powers instead.

Rome also had the mundus, a pit or chamber thought to connect with the underworld. On three days a year, 24 August, 5 October and 8 November, it was opened, and people said “the mundus is open”: the dead could come out, and public business was avoided. These days are sometimes kept by modern Roman polytheists as days to honour the dead and the gods below.

knowAndDont.known: Pausanias 6.25.2 describes the shrine at Elis. The Eleusinian Plutonion and the Hierapolis Plutonion are excavated. Odyssey 10 and 11 describe chthonic offering in detail. Roman sources (Macrobius, Festus) mention the mundus and its three opening days.
knowAndDont.unknown: How common private offerings to Hades were is unknown; most evidence concerns the dead in general or Plouton with the Two Goddesses. Scholars now stress that the line between sky and earth gods was a spectrum, not a rule, and practices varied by city.

lessons.inPractice: Modern Hellenic devotees approach Hades rarely and carefully: at night, with libations poured into the earth, hands lowered, and often only alongside Persephone. Many give to him once a month at most, and at times of death and mourning. This journey follows that rhythm.
reflect: Why do you think the Greeks felt they did not need to court Hades?
How does it feel to make an offering you will never take back?
further: Pausanias, Description of Greece 6.25.2, trans. W. H. S. Jones (1918)
Homer, Odyssey 10.516–540 and 11.23–50, trans. Samuel Butler (1900)
Gunnel Ekroth, The Sacrificial Rituals of Greek Hero-Cults (2002), on chthonic sacrifice

lessons.title: Hades today, and a shrine apart
lessons.summary: Who honours him now, grief and death work, the pop-culture Hades, and how to set up a separate shrine.

sections.heading: Who honours him now
sections.body:
Among Hellenic polytheists, Hades is honoured more than he was in antiquity, but still with care. Some keep him only as Plouton, the god of the earth’s wealth. Others honour him with Persephone as rulers of the dead, especially at funerals, anniversaries and the Anthesteria. A few devote themselves to him closely, often people who work with death: hospice workers, nurses, funeral directors, grief counsellors, and those who have lost many people.

Eclectic Pagans and witches sometimes honour him at Samhain as a god of the dead, or in shadow work. Many people now come to him through modern stories, especially romantic retellings of the Persephone myth and the video game Hades. That is a real way in, and nobody should be ashamed of it. But it is worth reading the old sources and letting the ancient god replace the character.

sections.heading: Grief
sections.body:
Hades is a steady god for the grieving. He does not promise to give your dead back, and he does not lie about death. What devotees often ask is that he keep their dead well, that Persephone receive them kindly, and that they themselves be able to bear the loss. Pouring a libation into the earth and saying the name of someone you have lost is one of the oldest acts of Greek religion.

If you are grieving, also look after yourself in ordinary ways. Eat, sleep, talk to people, and seek a bereavement service or counsellor if the weight does not lift. If you feel drawn to Hades because you want to be with your dead, or because you are thinking about ending your life, please contact a crisis line (988 in the US, Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, or your local emergency number) or a doctor today. He is a god of the dead, not a god who calls the living to die.

sections.heading: A shrine apart
sections.body:
Greek practice kept the gods below a little apart from the gods of the house. If you set up a shrine to Hades, put it somewhere separate from your main household shrine, Hestia’s hearth or kitchen: a low shelf, a corner, a box you open only for his rites. Many devotees keep it low to the ground, which suits a god of the earth.

On it you might put a dish of soil, a small lamp, a key, a cypress sprig or a dried pomegranate, a stone such as obsidian or onyx, and the card with your dead’s names. Black, deep red and dark purple are modern colour choices. Keep a separate cup and dish for his libations, and never use them for food. Many devotees also keep a small image of Persephone beside him.

sections.heading: What not to do
sections.body:
Do not eat or drink anything you have offered him. Do not offer him the leftovers of a meal; give him a fresh portion or nothing. Do not try to summon the dead through him, or use him in curses. Greek curse tablets sometimes named the gods below, and this journey does not follow them. Ask him for protection, for the peace of the dead, for justice, and for steadiness. Leave the rest to him.

And do not make him a constant companion if that weighs on you. It is entirely traditional to honour Hades only a few times a year, or only at times of death. A relationship with him does not need to be daily to be real.

knowAndDont.known: Modern Hellenic devotion to Hades is documented in community writing and practice; its chthonic forms draw on ancient sources. Curse tablets invoking the underworld gods are well known from antiquity. Separation of chthonic and household cult is an old principle.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no ancient evidence for a personal, daily devotion to Hades of the kind some modern devotees keep; it is a modern development. Colours and crystals for him are modern.

lessons.inPractice: Set up his shrine apart from the household shrine this week. Choose a separate cup and dish. Add the card with your dead’s names. If you also honour Persephone, place her image beside him.
reflect: Where in your home feels right for a god who is kept apart?
What do you hope Hades will keep for you?
further: Robert Garland, The Greek Way of Death (2nd ed., 2001)

practices.title: Read the Nekyia
practices.instructions: Once in this stage, read Odyssey book 11, Odysseus’s visit to the dead, in Samuel Butler’s free translation. Notice the pit, the libations and the dead who come to drink.
practices.prompt: What struck me about the way Odysseus approached the dead?

practices.title: Set up a shrine apart
practices.instructions: After the fourth lesson, set up a small, low shrine apart from your household gods: a dish of soil, a lamp, a key or cypress, a separate cup, and the card with your dead’s names.
practices.prompt: Where did I place his shrine, and what is on it?

stages.title: Nine nights of remembrance
stages.intro: Greeks made offerings at a grave on the third and ninth days after a death. This stage follows that old pattern: nine nights of a short, quiet remembrance, with libations poured into the earth on the third and ninth nights only, then a lesson on his days and offerings. It is deliberately spare.

lessons.title: His days, his offerings, and the rules of not sharing
lessons.summary: When to honour Hades, what to give, the full chthonic libation, and why nothing is shared or reused.

sections.heading: His days
sections.body:
Hades had no great festival of his own in Athens. The days that suit him are the days of the dead. The third day of the Anthesteria, the Chytroi, was given to the dead and to Hermes of the underworld, and ended with the spirits being sent away. The Genesia, in early autumn, was a day for honouring dead parents. Many modern devotees also honour the gods below at the end of each lunar month, alongside Hekate’s Deipnon, when the house is cleansed.

He was honoured with Persephone and Demeter at Eleusis. In the Roman calendar, the Parentalia in February and the Lemuria in May were festivals of the dead, and the mundus opened three times a year. And of course there are the days in your own life: funerals, anniversaries of deaths, and the ninth and thirtieth days after a loss.

sections.heading: What to give
sections.body:
The classic chthonic libation is the one in the Odyssey: honey mixed with milk, then wine, then water, with barley sprinkled over. Honey and milk were sometimes called melikraton. Wine may be dark and unmixed for the dead, or you may use dark grape juice or skip it. Other fitting gifts are pomegranate, barley, dark bread, a little myrrh or frankincense, and coins, which were placed with the dead to pay Charon the ferryman.

Many modern devotees also give to him by caring for the dead: tending a neglected grave, giving to a hospice, volunteering for a death café or a funeral fund for people who cannot afford one. These are good offerings for the receiver of many.

sections.heading: Not shared, not reused
sections.body:
Offerings to Hades are given away entirely. You do not eat or drink them, and they are not shared at a meal afterwards. This is the strongest rule of chthonic worship, and it reflects the idea that what goes to the dead belongs to the dead. Pour into bare earth, a pit you dig and fill again, a plant pot, or a dish of soil you will tip outside. If you burn something, let it burn completely and bury the ash.

Keep his vessels apart: a cup and a dish used for nothing else. Do not put them in the kitchen with everyday plates. Wash your hands after his rites, and turn back to the living with a word to Hestia, a glass of water or a bite of food. The Greeks purified themselves after contact with death, and this simple return is a modern version of that care.

sections.heading: Pouring well
sections.body:
A full chthonic pour goes like this. Kneel or crouch at the earth after dark. Wash your hands. Lay your palms on the ground or turn them down. Speak quietly, using his titles. Pour the honey-milk, then the wine or juice, then the water, each slowly, turning your face a little aside. Sprinkle a pinch of barley. Say what you have given and that you take nothing back. Sit for a moment. Then stand, wash your hands, and go indoors without lingering.

You do not need to do this often. Once a month is plenty for most people, and many give to Hades only a few times a year. The care with which you do it matters more than how often.

knowAndDont.known: The Odyssey gives the honey-milk, wine, water and barley sequence. The Anthesteria’s Chytroi, the Genesia and the third and ninth day grave offerings are attested for Athens. Charon’s obol, the coin for the ferryman, is attested in literature and graves, though not universal.
knowAndDont.unknown: Many details of private offering to Hades are lost. Whether every chthonic offering was strictly unshared is now debated by scholars, who find some exceptions. Modern monthly rhythms are modern choices.

lessons.inPractice: In the nine nights below, pour fully on the third and ninth nights only. On the other nights, simply sit at his shrine and say the names of your dead. Choose one act of care for the dead to do this month, such as tending a grave or giving to a hospice.
reflect: What does it feel like to give something entirely away, with nothing back?
Who among your dead would you like Hades to keep well?
further: Robert Garland, The Greek Way of Death (2nd ed., 2001)
Jon D. Mikalson, Ancient Greek Religion (2nd ed., 2010)

practices.title: Nine nights of remembrance
practices.instructions: For nine nights, at about the same time after dark, go to his shrine. Wash your hands. Light the lamp and speak Hestia’s name. Lower your hands toward the soil. Say one of his titles, then say aloud the name of one of your dead, or, if you have none, simply sit with the thought of all the dead who came before you. Sit for three minutes in silence. On the third and ninth nights, pour a full libation into the earth: honey-milk, then wine or juice, then water, with a pinch of barley. Do not drink any of it. Afterwards, wash your hands, speak Hestia’s name, put out the lamp, and drink a glass of water.
practices.prompt: Whose name did I say tonight? What did the silence hold?

stages.title: At the river
stages.intro:
In the old stories the dead cross a river and do not come back. You, however, can turn around. Take a few days to look honestly at this month before deciding anything.

Stopping here is a good outcome. So is pausing, or deciding to honour Hades only now and then, with Persephone, or turning to another god, another path, or none. Many devoted Hellenic polytheists never dedicate themselves to Hades at all and still honour him with great respect. That is a fine way to keep him.

practices.title: A walk among the dead
practices.instructions: Walk through a cemetery or churchyard in daylight, quietly and respectfully. Read a few names. Ask yourself whether you want the king of the dead as a lasting part of your life, or whether respect from a distance is right for you.
practices.prompt: What did I feel among the graves? Which answer felt true?

questions: Did I keep the nine nights because I wanted to, or because I felt I had to?
Am I drawn to the ancient Hades, or mainly to a modern character from a film, game or book? Is that enough?
Is my pull toward Hades connected to thoughts of my own death? If so, have I spoken to someone about it?
Does honouring him leave me steadier, or more weighed down? Would occasional honour suit me better than dedication?
Can I keep the rule of not sharing his offerings and keeping his things apart, for a year?
Would I be relieved or disappointed if I chose to wait? What does that tell me?

stages.title: The dedication at the earth
stages.intro:
If you have chosen to go on, make your dedication after dark at the end of a lunar month, on the anniversary of a death that matters to you, or at the Anthesteria. This is a self-dedication, a promise you make on your own behalf. It is not an initiation, and it does not make you a priest or initiate of anything. It does not replace the rites of any group that initiates.

It is also a promise to a god who was rarely given such promises. Keep it modest. Ancient Greeks did not dedicate themselves to Hades; they honoured him with care. Your promise can be simply to keep that care.

rite.title: Self-dedication to Hades
rite.summary: Purify, begin with Hestia, kneel at the earth with lowered hands, call Hades by his titles with Persephone beside him, make your promise, pour the full chthonic libation, give a coin, and return to the living.

ingredients.name: A bowl of fresh water and a match or bay sprig for khernips
A small lamp, tealight or electric candle
Honey mixed with milk, a little dark wine or grape juice, and water, in separate cups
Bare earth, a plant pot, or his dish of soil
The card with the names of your dead
Your written promise on a card
A little myrrh on a heatproof burner

rite.preparation: Write your promise in your own words, modest and doable: for example, to honour Hades and Persephone at the Anthesteria and on the anniversaries of my dead, to keep his offerings unshared and his things apart, to speak of death honestly, and to care for the dead and the dying where I can. Clean his shrine. Wash and dress plainly. If you are going outside, tell someone and take a torch.

steps.title: Purify
steps.instructions: Make khernips by quenching the flame in the water. Wash your hands and touch your face.
steps.spoken: With clean hands I come to the edge of the ground.

steps.title: Begin with Hestia
steps.instructions: Light the lamp. Speak to Hestia before turning to the world below.
steps.spoken: Hestia, first and last, I begin with you.

steps.title: Call the king below
steps.instructions: Kneel at the earth. Lay your palms on the ground, or strike it gently three times, as Greeks did to be heard below. Add myrrh if you are using it. Keep your voice low.
steps.spoken: Plouton, Hades, Zeus of the earth, unseen king, receiver of many, good counsellor, keeper of the keys: hear me. And Persephone, dread queen, beside him: hear me. This month I have kept your silence and said the names of my dead. Now I come to make a promise.

steps.title: Make your promise
steps.instructions: Read your promise aloud, quietly and clearly. Then read the names on the card.
steps.spoken: This is my promise, made freely. Keep my dead well.

steps.title: Pour the threefold libation
steps.instructions: Turning your face a little aside, pour the honey-milk into the earth, then the wine or juice, then the water. Sprinkle the barley over all. Nothing is kept back and nothing is drunk.
steps.spoken: I give this, and take nothing back.

steps.title: Give the coin
steps.instructions: Press the coin into the soil, or lay it in his dish, for the ferryman and for the wealthy one below. It stays there.

steps.title: Sit in silence
steps.instructions: Sit quietly with lowered hands for a while.

steps.title: Return to the living
steps.instructions: Stand. Wash your hands again in the khernips. Turn toward the house and speak Hestia’s name. Put out the lamp. Go indoors and drink a glass of water or eat a little bread.
steps.spoken: Hestia, last as you were first. I return to the living. It is done.

rite.closing: Leave the libation and coin in the earth. If you used a dish indoors, take it outside the next day and tip the soil onto ground, leaving the coin with it. Keep your written promise on his shrine and read it each year at the Anthesteria. Write in your journal what you promised, and then do something ordinary and alive: call a friend, take a walk, cook.
rite.safety: Never leave a flame unattended; use a lantern or electric candle outdoors. Tell someone if you go out after dark and keep to safe places. Myrrh smoke can affect asthma and pets. Wash your hands after handling soil. Do not leave wine or honey where pets or wildlife can reach it in quantity.

stages.title: Keeping the silence
stages.intro:
Your relationship with Hades now lives in a few careful moments each year. Honour him and Persephone at the Anthesteria, on the anniversaries of your dead, and, if you like, once a month at the end of the lunar month. Pour into the earth, take nothing back, and turn again to the living.

Once a year, at the Anthesteria or on your dedication anniversary, read your promise and renew it, change it, or set it down with thanks. If months pass without an offering, that is in keeping with his oldest worship. When you need him, kneel at the ground and say his name, or Plouton’s, and he will be where he always is.

practices.title: A monthly pour, if you wish
practices.instructions: At the end of each lunar month, after Hekate’s Deipnon if you keep it, pour honey-milk and water into the earth for Hades and Persephone and say the names of your dead. Skip months freely.
practices.prompt: Who did I remember this month?

practices.title: Anniversaries of the dead
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of a death that matters to you, pour the threefold libation into the earth, say their name, and do one act of care for the dead or the dying.
practices.prompt: What did I carry for them this year?

practices.title: Yearly rededication
practices.instructions: At the Anthesteria or on your dedication anniversary, repeat the dedication rite with your promise rewritten for the year ahead.
practices.prompt: What has a year of honouring the king below taught me about death and about living?
